newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway's new premier unlikely to change policies.
newsitem.headline: Norway's new premier unlikely to change policies.

text.p: Norway's next prime minister, Thorbjoern Jagland, will seek to pursue the middle-of-the-road policies of his predecessor, Gro Harlem Brundtland, despite a reputation of being a leftist, political analysts say.

But they are waiting to see whether Jagland will have the political clout that the veteran Brundtland, who announced her resignation on Wednesday, has had in the ruling Labour Party and a hostile parliament.
Jagland, who takes over as premier of the minority government on Friday, has been chairman of the Labour Party since 1992 and has been groomed as Brundtland's successor for a year.
His support for continued state ownership of the top commercial banks has won him few friends in the markets, which reacted nervously to news of his appointment.
"He is seen as more closely related to the unions than the former prime minister was," said London-based Keld Holm, a Lehman Brothers international economist.

Holm said Norway, one of the few European countries to enjoy a budget surplus, needed a strong prime minister who could say "no' to the unions. "Clearly, Jagland has a reputation of being slightly less tough," he added.
Financial analyst Oeystein Stephansen, of Oslo-based S-E Banken, said: "Many have judged him wrongly. He is going to be different as prime minister.

"We will not see nationalisations. We will see a new leader trying to build up his credentials. But the government policy is laid down by the Labour Party congress and there will not be any changes to it."

Brundtland told a news conference there would be no change in economic or other policies as a result of the shift of power. "The Labour Party's principal targets will remain employment, welfare and concern for future generations," she said.
Nils Morten Udgaard, foreign editor of Aftenposten, Norway's most influential daily, said: "I think Jagland will try to stand as strongly as Brundtland.
"But Norwegian markets are worried he will not be as tough in defending the budget at a time when Norway enjoys a great surplus."
Brundtland, 57, anxious to ensure stability in the politics of the oil-rich Scandinavian state, publicly named 46-year-old Jagland as her successor a year ago.
But Wednesday's sudden announcement that she was handing over power to Jagland in two days caught markets on the hop.
The crown weakened but recovered quickly to close virtually unchanged from Tuesday and Norwegian bonds were little affected.
The announcement also surprised markets because it came in the midst of 1997 budget negotiations.
The government is under pressure from the opposition right and left-of-centre to increase expenditure in the draft budget, which projects a 40.9 billion crown ($6.32 billion) surplus.
Despite the surplus, the government has said it will keep a tight grip on its purse for fear of fuelling inflation.

Kjetil Groenskag, head of Norwegian research at Alfred Berg in London, forecast short-term uncertainty on the markets, at least until Jagland has been appointed in the next few days and perhaps until the 1997 budget is approved in December.
But Groenskag added: "Jagland has informally been a kind of prime minister-trainee for the past couple of years."
As such, he said, Jagland had been learning to make his leftist views more palatable for the markets. ($1=6.468 Norwegian Crown)
